'''''Lycium chinense''''' is one of two species of [[boxthorn]] [[shrub]] in the family [[Solanaceae]]. Along with ''[[Lycium barbarum]]'', it produces the [[Goji|goji berry ("wolfberry")]]. Two varieties are recognized,<ref name=flochi>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200020538|title=Flora of China treatment for ''L. chinense''}}</ref> ''L. chinense'' var. ''chinense'' and  ''L. chinense'' var. ''potaninii''. It is also known as '''Chinese boxthorn''', '''Chinese matrimony-vine''', '''Chinese teaplant''', '''Chinese wolfberry''', '''wolfberry''',<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate = 10 January 2018}}</ref> and '''Chinese desert-thorn'''.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=LYCH|taxon=Lycium chinense|accessdate=24 June 2015}}</ref>

== Description ==
Wolfberry species are [[deciduous]] [[wood]]y shrubs, growing {{convert|1|–|3|m}} high, somewhat shorter than ''L. barbarum''.  The stems are highly branched.  Branches are pale gray, slender, curved or pendulous, with thorns {{convert|0.5|–|2|cm}} long.<ref name=flochi/>

=== Leaves ===
''Lycium chinense'' leaves form on the shoot either solitary in an alternating arrangement or in bundles of 2 to 4.  Their [[glossary of leaf morphology|shape]] may be ovate, rombic, lanceolate, or linear-lanceolate, usually {{convert|1.5|-|5|cm}} long and {{convert|0.5|-|2.5|cm}} wide (but up to {{convert|10|cm}} long and {{convert|4|cm}} wide in cultivated plants).<ref name=flochi/>

===Flowers===
The flowers grow in groups of one to three in the leaf [[axil]]s, with [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s {{convert|1|-|2|cm}} long.<ref name=flochi/>  The bell-shaped or tubular [[sepal|calyx]] (eventually ruptured by the growing berry) splits halfway into short, triangular, densely ciliate lobes. The [[Corolla (flower)|corollae]] is a tube that splits into lavender or light purple  [[petal]]s, {{convert|9-14|mm|abbr=on}} wide with five or six lobes longer than the tube, with short hairs at the edge. The [[stamens]] are structured with [[wikt:Filaments|filaments]] longer than the [[anthers]], slightly shorter or longer than the corolla, with a villous ring slightly above the base and the adjacent corolla tube.<ref name=flochi/> The anthers are longitudinally [[dehiscence (botany)|dehiscent]].

=== Fruit and seeds ===
''Lycium chinense'' produces a bright orange-red berry, whose [[Glossary of botanical terms#O|shape is ovoid or oblong]], {{convert|7|-|15|mm}} long and 5 to 8 mm wide (but up to {{convert|22|mm}} long and {{convert|10|mm}} wide in cultivation).<ref name=flochi/> It contains compressed yellow seeds, from 2.5 to 3 mm wide, with a curved embryo; their number varies widely based on [[cultivar]] and fruit size, from 10 to 60.  The berries ripen from July to October in the [[Northern Hemisphere]].

===Disease===
It can be parasitized by the oomycete species ''[[Peronospora lycii]]''.<ref name=Constantinescu>{{cite journal |last1= Constantinescu |first= O. |title= An annotated list of ''[[Peronospora]]'' names |date= 1991 |journal= Thunbergia |volume= 15}}</ref>

===Similar species===
''Lycium chinense'' can be distinguished from the very similar ''Lycium barbarum'' by morphological traits of the flowers. The corolla tubes of ''barbarum'' are significantly longer than the lobes, and the calyx of ''chinense'' usually has more than two lobes whereas ''barbarum'' has just two.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

== Use ==
The fruits may be infused with hot water to make [[goji tea]]. The plant has been used for centuries in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] for treating various disorders,{{citation needed|date=March 2020}} although there is no [[evidence-based medicine|high-quality clinical evidence]] that consuming it has any effect on health or disease.

==Chemistry==
The fruit composition is similar to that of ''L. barbarum'', with  [[polysaccharide]]s, [[carotenoid]]s and [[flavonoid]]s as main constituents.<ref name=potterat>{{cite journal|author=Olivier Potterat|year=2010|title=Goji (''Lycium barbarum'' and ''L. chinense''): Phytochemistry, pharmacology and safety in the perspective of traditional uses and recent popularity|journal=Planta Medica|volume=76|issue=1|pages=7–19|doi=10.1055/s-0029-1186218|pmid=19844860|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[Rutin]] is a prominent flavonoid, while the main carotenoid is [[zeaxanthin]] [[palmitic acid|dipalmitate]] (49% of the carotenoid fraction), with [[β-carotene]], two [[cerebroside]]s, and three [[pyrrole]] derivatives as other constituents.<ref name=potterat/>

Dozens of secondary [[metabolite]]s have been isolated and identified from the roots, root bark, and leaves, including cyclic peptides, [[alkaloid]]s, and flavonoids.<ref name=potterat/> [[Citric acid]] is the major nonvolatile organic acid in the leaves followed by [[oxalic acid]].<ref name=potterat/>
